**An agent carries a token**

work-unit · 2026-08-25

discharges: [MUS-M-0012](../milestones.md#mus-m-0012)

raised by: [MUS-Q-0051](../questions.md#mus-q-0051)

after: [MUS-W-0020](MUS-W-0020.md#mus-w-0020)

mandate: [MUS-M-0002](../milestones.md#mus-m-0002)

## Context

Milestone 5c: the credential an agent can hold. 5b built a guard and could not switch it on, because /mcp is on the guarded mux, an MCP call is a POST, and an agent has no passkey. A token is issued at the command line, carried in a header, scoped to one path and one project, and revoked immediately.

## Done means

An agent reaches the mandated tool call on a server started with --accounts, carrying a token and no session cookie. A token is printed once and stored only as a hash; there is nothing to look up and a lost token is reissued and the old one revoked. A token can be revoked, and it stops working on the running server rather than at the next restart. A revoked token leaves its row behind, so a listing can still say it existed and when it stopped. A token is not a passkey: it opens /mcp and nothing else, and an owner-roled token still cannot read the records surface or sign in. A token is scoped to a project, like every other role here; one issued for another project is refused. Rubbish in the Authorization header is refused rather than mistaken for anything, and an absent header is refused exactly as a revoked one is. The startup banner does not advertise a tool-call URL that refuses: with --accounts on it names the header, and it says when no token is live. A token id is safe to type at a shell.

## Verified against

Tests, plus the whole thing against a running server on 127.0.0.1:7951 with --accounts enforced. Measured there, in order: POST /mcp with no credential 403; with a token 200; a full MCP handshake — initialize, notifications/initialized, tools/call — returning this repository's routing in full; GET /records with the same token 303 to /signin rather than through. Then, without restarting: mustur account revoke, and the same token 403 on the same process. The listing shows the token before as last used and after as revoked. In tests: a real MCP client through the real guard rather than a bare POST, because tools/list before initialize is refused by the protocol and would have proved nothing about the guard (TestAnAgentReachesTheToolCallWithATokenAndNoCookie). Both negative tests were mutation-checked. Widening the guard's scope from /mcp to everything makes TestATokenOpensTheToolCallAndNothingElse fail; making ByToken ignore the revoked column makes TestRevokingATokenStopsItAtOnce fail. The scope test first passed for the wrong reason: its client followed the guard's 303 to /signin and reported 200 on a public page. It now follows no redirects and asserts 303 or 403 rather than not-200. The guard lets a token past /mcp with no write check, which is only safe while every tool on that surface reads. internal/mcpsrv's own test asserts exactly one tool named mustur_route and now says why, so adding a second fails there and names the guard.

## Risks

Nothing here is deployed. The running service passes neither --origin nor --accounts, and issuing the deployment's own token is the owner's act. A token has no expiry, deliberately: an invitation expires because it is a link in transit and a session expires because a browser is borrowed, but an agent token is configuration, and a credential that stops at 3am without anybody deciding that is an outage rather than a control. Revocation is the control and it is immediate. A token is a long-lived secret in a systemd unit or a process environment, which is a weaker place than a device's secure element. Scope is what makes that acceptable: one path, one project, no browser surface. Widening the scope later would be widening the blast radius of that weaker secret. The guard consults the token before the account, so a request carrying both a valid token and a session cookie is answered as the agent. That is deliberate on /mcp and reaches nowhere else, but it is a precedence rule rather than an obvious truth. last_used is written on every accepted call and is best-effort: a failure to record it does not refuse a valid credential. It is a convenience for deciding which of several tokens is safe to revoke, not an audit trail. Cloudflare Access is still in front and its removal is still the owner's judgement (MUS-Q-0039). This milestone removes the reason --accounts could not be turned on; it does not turn it on.
